packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.content: `start()` awaits each provider sequentially inside the loop; a provider whose `start()` never settles will block every later provider from starting and will hang the caller indefinitely. Starting providers is independent work, so await them with `Promise.all` (or at least race each with a timeout) to avoid one bad provider stalling the whole manager.

`stop()` tears down subscriptions and stops providers but does not cancel timers already queued through `schedule` (nor does `restart` consult `this.started`). A restart scheduled before shutdown still fires afterwards, calling `provider.stop().then(() => provider.start())` — resurrecting a provider and mutating `statuses`/`restarts` after the manager is stopped, which leaks resources and produces invalid state transitions. Track scheduled timer handles/handlers and cancel or no-op them in `stop()` (e.g. guard the callback with `if (!this.started) return;`).

`restart()` has no per-provider in-flight guard. Two `failed` statuses arriving before the scheduled callback runs (or the recursive `this.restart(provider)` in the `.catch` below firing while a prior attempt is still pending) will each increment `restarts`, schedule duplicate timers, and consume the restart budget twice for a single failure. Track an in-flight flag/set keyed by `provider.id` and ignore re-entrant restart requests until the current attempt settles.

`Promise.all([...this.restartsInFlight])` snapshots the set once. A restart chained from a failure `.catch` (which calls `this.restart` → adds a new promise + schedules a new timer) is added *after* the snapshot, so `settleRestarts` can resolve while a recursively scheduled restart is still pending — tests/shutdown will observe incomplete failover. Loop until the set is empty (draining newly added entries) instead of awaiting a single snapshot.

The `reason` union declares `"quality"` but no code path ever emits it; `pick()`/`emitSwitch` only ever pass `acquired`, `higher-authority`, or `stale-takeover`. Consumers matching on `"quality"` switches will never fire. Either implement the quality-driven switch (e.g. when the holder's quality degrades relative to a challenger) or drop the unused member to keep the contract accurate.

`this.options` is built by spreading the whole `opts` object (typed `{ now } & Partial<FusionOptions>`), so the non-`FusionOptions` `now` callback is copied into `options` and then leaked by `getOptions()` (`{ ...this.options, authority: [...] }`), returning an object with an unexpected `now` property. Destructure `now` out before spreading, or spread only the known option keys.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/ax.ts.content: Play state is inferred from the *presence* of a node mentioning pause/play/cue, in tree order, with `pause`/`cue` tested before `play`. A tree that always contains a "Pause" (or "Cue") control, or a single transport toggle whose label lists both, forces `playing=false` even while a deck is playing. This does not read the toggle's actual state (AX/UIA checked/selected/TogglePattern). Prefer the toggle's checked state, and avoid treating mere presence of a "Pause"/"Cue" label as "not playing".

`timeToSeconds` applies a negative sign, so a remaining-time string like "-2:48" becomes `remainingSeconds = -168` instead of `168`. Because `isRemaining` also matches unsigned labeled remaining nodes, `remainingSeconds` has an inconsistent sign depending on how the UI renders it. Two concrete consequences: (a) the field no longer represents a remaining-time magnitude, and (b) it inverts `refineAxReading`'s "remaining decreases" checks — a signed countdown goes -168 -> -167 (i.e. numerically *increases*), so playing is never inferred from remaining for signed values. Downstream consumers that treat it as a magnitude (e.g. `ax-provider` using `remainingSeconds` as an elapsed fallback) then pass a negative value on. Normalize remaining to a positive magnitude and align the comparison direction, or make the sign explicit in the field semantics.

`all` is the fully flattened tree, so every node whose role matches `/deck|player/` — including a nested `role='player'` descendant of a deck container — becomes its own container, and the `/group|pane/` fallback matches many unrelated panels. The same deck can therefore produce multiple readings whose time nodes overlap, with colliding or renumbered `deckId`s (see `deckIndexOf`). Identify deck containers at one well-defined level (e.g. direct children of the deck area) and de-duplicate before reading.

The fallback derives deck identity from positional index in the container list. Since that list can contain nested/extra containers (see the container filter above), any such node shifts the numbering and produces incorrect `deckId`s and sort order rather than a stable identity. Additionally, `indexOf` returns -1 when the node is absent, silently yielding `deckId === 0`. Derive the deck number from an explicit label/attribute, and guard against a missing sibling instead of emitting a bogus id.

When both fields are present but no motion is observed (or `previous` is undefined), this returns `readable: true` while `playing` is left as whatever `current.playing` was — often `null`. That produces an inconsistent `{ readable: true, playing: null }` reading that callers treat as authoritative (the provider emits it and labels `playing` as only "estimated"). Either explicitly fall back to `current.playing`, or keep `readable` false when play/remaining state cannot be determined.

The binary search assumes `grid` is sorted ascending by `sourceTimeMs` and free of duplicate/gap entries, but nothing validates that. With an unsorted or duplicated grid the search silently returns a plausible-looking beat number (or 1 at the boundary) instead of `null`, corrupting the playhead mapping. Validate monotonicity (bail to `null`) or document/enforce the precondition at the call sites.
